hook.text: Each chime you hear is a leak: money a bug would cost.
One sandbox test run: eight leaks, $491.
Shakedown finds them first, for developers with PayPal checkouts.

store.text: My demo shop, Leaky Llama, has bugs on purpose.
A customer approves a payment, PayPal collects, and my shop ships.
PayPal also sends a “paid” message, signed to prove it’s real.
Skip one check: goods ship unpaid, or someone pays twice.

meet.text: Shakedown runs in PayPal’s sandbox: pretend money, nothing really ships.
Its five customers from hell are fixed scripts, not AI.
Four test my checkout; one tests my shop’s AI assistant, Lulu.

live.text: The Double-Clicker presses Pay twice, and pays $24 twice.
On another order, a retry ships it twice: another $24.
The Cart Shuffler picks its own price, and later swaps a cart: two leaks, $353.
The Echo sends unsigned “paid” messages three ways: once, twice, and late.
The Bouncer’s card is declined, but its order ships: $36.

proof.text: The Cart Shuffler approved $18 for socks.
Then it swapped in two pairs of saddlebags.
PayPal’s sandbox dashboard agrees: $18, for socks.
Its other leak: saddlebags worth $124, paid $1.

ai-vs-code.text: My policy: over $100 an order, a person decides.
In one recorded run, the Policy Lawyer asked Lulu for $124, in two parts.
Plain code read PayPal’s refunds: the second, $34, should have gone to a person.

fix.text: Each leak gets a fix, like shipping only what PayPal collected.
Two Echo checks stay inconclusive: only PayPal can sign those messages.
Shakedown runs from one command, or on every pull request.
A leak that comes back fails the check.

close.text: I tested the tester: every checkout bug I switched on was caught, with no false alarms.
Claude runs Lulu, reads my policy, and explains; plain code decides.
I also sent PayPal’s Agent Toolkit a fix for retried calls.
Shakedown: let customers from hell find your leaks first.
